question: How does Rachmaninoff separate the running figures from the broader middle?
intro: Rachmaninoff recorded this waltz for Victor in 1923. The transfer includes several seconds of silence after the music, so its two-minute file length is not the playing time.

sections.label: Running figures resume
sections.mNote: denser attacks return after the quieter middle

cues.title: A pianist on shellac
cues.text: Rachmaninoff plays a Steinway grand in this source attribution. Listen to the spacing of phrases rather than treating the restricted recorded tone as the full sound of his instrument.
cues.evidence: Commons names the Steinway and dates the recording 5 April 1923; DAHR matrix B-24192 lists that session and the issued take 5. No particular piano timbre is inferred from the analysis.

cues.title: The surface leaves more space
cues.text: Across this quieter stretch, the rapid surface gives way to more widely spaced attacks. Compare the melodic line with the accompaniment instead of assuming that fewer notes must mean a slower underlying waltz beat.
cues.evidence: The report marks a boundary at 0:36: detected attacks fall from 6–7 per second in the opening to roughly 4–5 at 0:35–1:05. The estimate describes activity, not beat tempo.

cues.title: The running surface returns
cues.text: The later span regains the closely spaced attacks of the opening and grows in recorded weight. Follow the phrase through its rise rather than counting every fast note as a separate accent.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 1:12 and 1:18 accompany a rise from −26 dB at 1:10 to −11.7 at 1:20; detected attacks rise to 6.8–7.2 per second.

cues.title: Music ends before the file
cues.text: After the final phrase, this transfer falls into silence. Compare musical endings between pianists before comparing file lengths: a digital tail is not rubato.
cues.evidence: The 1:50 window falls to −36.9 dB and the 1:55 and 2:00 windows are silent at −80 dB. Complete file duration is 121.5 seconds.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
